description:
Nóstos means “the return to home”, and it guides everything we do. We are a team that brings together software, embedded systems, robotics, and nutrition. When we face a problem, we don’t see a task or an obstacle: we see an opportunity to create real value, in space and on Earth. 

"Our goal is to bring everyone home whole".
summary:
In January 2026, NASA cut an ISS mission short for the first time in 25 years because of a crew member’s medical issue. ISS crews can come home within days; a crew heading to Mars cannot. On long missions, astronauts must be their own first line of health defense, yet they lack a companion built for that role.

Meet Luniverse, a virtual companion for astronauts’ physical health and emotional well-being. Its character, Lunito, talks by voice: it asks how they feel, reads their vital signs and runs a health assessment. A traffic light on Lunito’s belly turns in different colors and explains the status. If low mood and poor sleep persist for days, the light changes and Lunito suggests a calming task and encourages the astronaut to reach out to the crew.

In an emergency, Luniverse alerts the crew and guides first-response checks, such as securing the person, checking breathing and reading vitals. It logs every step and sends the case to Ground, accounting for communication delay. It never prescribes treatment; it helps the crew assess and stabilize until Earth replies.

In the Lunito Community, crew members see each other’s status lights and support one another against isolation. Sensors connect directly to the app via Bluetooth Low Energy, so Luniverse keeps working even when Earth is delayed or unreachable. Our prototype combines a real sensor with simulated indicators.

Luniverse turns health monitoring into autonomy, early detection and teamwork.
details:
The problem

Long-duration missions expose astronauts to radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment. As distance from Earth grows, so does the delay in medical support, and astronauts carry much of the responsibility for noticing changes in their own health. Existing tools tend to show raw numbers, but few help astronauts understand what those numbers mean or what to do about them, and almost none address emotional well-being alongside physical health.

What Luniverse does

Luniverse is a health monitoring app built around Lunito, a friendly virtual companion. Instead of asking astronauts to type or interpret charts, Lunito interacts by voice:

  • Lunito asks the astronaut how they feel, and the astronaut answers out loud.
  • Luniverse combines that self-report with vital signs collected from sensors.
  • Lunito runs a health assessment and delivers the result in plain language.
  • A traffic light on Lunito’s belly turns in different colors, and Lunito explains the level and gives a summary.

The system tracks indicators such as heart rate, sleep hours and mood, chosen because their ranges reflect how the mission’s hazards affect the body and mind.

Lunito Community

Each crew member sees their own Lunito and their teammates’ Lunitos with their status lights. This lets the crew notice when someone is struggling and support them, which matters in isolation and confinement. It also rewards healthy habits, and a tasks section gives astronauts concrete actions to improve their status, for example a calming activity when mood and sleep decline.

Emergency mode

When something goes wrong, any crew member can open an emergency case. Luniverse then:

  • Alerts the crew and shows the responder a step-by-step protocol as a checklist: secure the person and yourself, check responsiveness and breathing, place the sensor on their finger, and check the oxygen in the med kit.
  • Pulls live vital signs from the sensor (for example heart rate and SpO2) straight into a timestamped case log.
  • Lets the responder dictate notes by voice, so their hands stay free.
  • Sends the case to Ground and shows the expected communication delay with a countdown to the reply.
  • Keeps the case open if the responder leaves the screen, until they close it.

Luniverse does not diagnose or prescribe. Its role is to help the crew verify that the person is stable, document what happens, and act correctly during the minutes or hours before Earth can reply. The protocol shown in the prototype is a sample pending validation by medical experts.

How it works technically

  • Sensors send data directly to the app via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). The app is installable and caches its content offline, so core screens and sensor data remain available without a connection.
  • AI voice features (speech-to-text, conversation and text-to-speech) currently run on Cloudflare Workers AI and need a connection. Moving them on-device is the next step toward a fully offline experience.
  • When a link is available, emergency cases are sent to Ground, with communication delay built into the flow.
  • Hardware representation: an ESP32-C3 microcontroller paired with a real pulse and oxygen sensor (MAX30102) transmitting over BLE. Other indicators are simulated to demonstrate the complete experience.
  • The same pipeline can accept additional sensors or wearables, so monitoring can grow without redesigning the system.

Software and tools

  • Front end: React 19, TypeScript and Vite
  • Interface: Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Lucide icons
  • Charts: Recharts and custom SVG graphics
  • Lunito in 3D: Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei; character model created with Meshy and Blender
  • Backend and hosting: Cloudflare Workers with a TypeScript API
  • AI: Cloudflare Workers AI, using Whisper for speech-to-text, Llama for conversation and data extraction, and MeloTTS for Lunito’s voice
  • Storage: data is stored locally on the device today; shared storage with Cloudflare D1 is planned
  • Installable app: Progressive Web App (PWA) with offline caching
  • Testing and quality: Vitest, Testing Library and Playwright for tests; Oxlint, Prettier and type checking for code quality
  • Development tools: Node.js, pnpm and GitHub Actions

Benefits and intended impact

  • Autonomy: astronauts can understand and act on their own and others’ health status without waiting for Earth.
  • Early detection: tracking trends helps catch deterioration before it forces a mission to end, as happened on the ISS in January 2026.
  • Emergency readiness: bridges the gap between an incident and Earth’s reply, giving the crew a structured response and a complete record when delay makes real-time support impossible.
  • Emotional support: mental health is treated as a core indicator, not an afterthought.
  • Teamwork: the crew looks after each other, which strengthens cohesion.
  • Beyond space: the same approach could help people in isolated environments on Earth, such as remote communities or expeditions.

What makes it creative

Most health tools are dashboards. Luniverse is a companion. A character that speaks, shows its status in a single visual signal and connects the crew turns monitoring into something astronauts want to use. This matters in missions where fatigue, stress and isolation make complex interfaces harder to use.

Factors we considered

  • Connectivity: core features are designed to stay available offline, and the emergency flow accounts for communication delay with Ground.
  • Usability under stress: voice interaction and a simple traffic-light signal reduce the mental effort of checking health.
  • Safety: Luniverse supports first response without diagnosing or prescribing, and its protocols are designed to be validated by medical professionals.
  • Scope: we cover the mission’s hazards partially, by monitoring variables whose ranges reflect their effects, and we designed the system to scale by adding more variables.
  • Prototype limits: with limited time, we used one real sensor and simulated the rest. Voice and conversation run in the cloud for now, and shared storage is still planned. We chose open-weight models so that both can move on-device.
